The increased national feeling and democratic ideas created tension between the Danish-speaking and the German-speaking parts of the population.
The population in Holstein was German, and most Danish politicians saw it as natural that the Holsteiners wanted to break away from Denmark and join the German Confederation.

But in Schleswig there were both Danish speakers, who wanted to remain part of Denmark, and German-speaking inhabitants, who wanted to break away and join the German Confederation together with Holstein.
This was called the Schleswig problem.
People and politicians on both sides of the border discussed where the Danish border should run.
In 1848, Schleswig and Holstein were refused their demand for an independent free constitution.

The German Confederation and the strongest of the German states, Prussia, backed the rebels and sent a large number of soldiers into the war on the side of the duchies.
In 1849 Denmark and the Schleswig-Holsteiners fought a series of battles.

In 1850, the German Confederation and Prussia were pressured by Russia to withdraw their auxiliary troops from the conflict.

In 1863, pressed by public opinion, the Danish Rigsdag adopted a new joint constitution for both Denmark and Schleswig, but not for Holstein.
The German states saw the Danish-Schleswig constitution as a breach of the agreement that had been made.
Prussia, whose political leader was the powerful prime minister Otto von Bismarck, therefore declared war on Denmark together with Austria in February 1864.
This war is called the Second Schleswig War.
Unlike the First Schleswig War in 1848 to 50, this time Denmark did not get help from the European great powers.
Denmark was attacked from the south, and the Danish forces expected that Dannevirke would protect them against the attack.
Dannevirke was a defensive structure which, since the Viking Age, had been a strong line of defence.
But in February 1864, the Danish army had to be evacuated in great haste from Dannevirke, because the opponents outnumbered them.

The defeat in 1864 was a catastrophe for Denmark.
Denmark had to cede Schleswig, Holstein and the small duchy of Lauenburg to Prussia and Austria.

The great majority of the population spoke the same language, had the same constitution, and were culturally quite alike, though there was still a great difference between rich and poor.

In 1871, Bismarck had gathered the German states into a strong empire, and Denmark now stood completely in the shadow of its large neighbour to the south.

To secure its continued survival, Denmark tried at almost any price to avoid involvement in international conflicts.
In security policy, Denmark afterwards chose to be strictly neutral, and maintained only a weak military defence.

The end of the 1800s and the beginning of the 1900s were marked by a far-reaching modernisation of Danish society.
Industrial development got going, prosperity rose, and new political reforms were meant to secure a freer economy.
Domestically, a marked conflict arose between the landowners' party, Højre, and the farmers' party, Venstre.

Industrialisation began in England already in the middle of the 1700s.
The most important causes were the development of the steam engine, the first railways at the beginning of the 1800s, and access to energy in the form of large coal reserves.
The first railway within Denmark's present borders opened in 1847, and ran between Copenhagen and Roskilde.
But industrialisation only really broke through in the second half of the 1800s.
And only after the Second World War did Denmark go from being an agricultural society to being a real industrial society.
So around 1850, and for a long time after, most Danes still earned their living in agriculture.
The beginning of industrialisation made large parts of the population move from the countryside into the towns, to work in industry or in crafts.
This created a completely new group in society: workers.
They often worked in the new factories or workshops in the town, and lived in small apartments in large apartment buildings.
The many industrial workers had common interests.
They wanted, among other things, to secure the highest possible wage for their work, reasonable working hours, and better safety in the workplace.
In October 1871, the International Workers' Association for Denmark was founded, as part of the international socialist movement that sought to influence workers in many countries.
In newspapers and on leaflets, the movement's leaders called for strikes and demonstrations to demand better conditions and higher pay for workers.
On their side, the employers held on to their right to manage and distribute the work.
The period was therefore marked by strikes and clashes.
The best-known clash between demonstrating workers and the authorities was the Battle of the Fælleden, which took place in May 1872.
It was a big workers' meeting in Copenhagen that ended in fighting between police and soldiers on one side, and workers on the other.
Nobody was killed at Fælleden, but many were imprisoned.
A political workers' party also emerged: the Social Democrats, Socialdemokratiet.
At the beginning it was part of the labour movement, but in 1878 it became an independent party.

Then comes one of the most important agreements in Danish history.

A long dispute in 1899 between employers and workers ended in September the same year with a historic agreement, the September Compromise, Septemberforliget, between the labour market's two main organisations, which today are called DA, the Danish Employers' Confederation, and FH, the Danish Trade Union Confederation.
With the agreement, the employers kept their right to manage and distribute the work.
And the workers got the right to organise and to look after their interests collectively, through trade unions and shop stewards.
For example, to negotiate pay and working conditions, or to strike according to specific rules.
The September Compromise still underlies the way agreements are made on the Danish labour market.
This way of agreeing things in Denmark is called "the Danish Model".
Now, a change in the countryside.
While industry grew in the towns, changes also happened in the countryside.
In the middle of the 1800s, Denmark had exported large amounts of grain.
But the situation changed in the middle of the 1870s.
Now steamships and railways made it possible for the USA and the Eastern European countries to export cheap grain to Western Europe, which made grain prices fall drastically.
So Danish farmers largely chose to switch to animal production.
That means raising, for example, cattle and pigs, to produce, among other things, butter and bacon, which quickly became Denmark's by far largest exports.
The most important market was Great Britain, which alone took more than half of the animal food exports in the period 1890 to 1914.

Farmers joined forces to set up, among other things, dairies and cooperative stores.

At the same time, through the cooperative movement's businesses, farmers could improve the quality of the goods.
A guiding principle of the cooperative movement was that members voted by "heads, not hooves".
It meant that a farmer, one head, who had only a few animals, hooves, formally had as much say as a big farmer with many animals.
Cooperative slaughterhouses were also set up, which gave farmers control over both production and sale of their meat.
The cooperative movement meant a lot for the development of Danish agriculture and for Denmark as a whole.
The democratic principles and the idea of equality that underlay the cooperative idea later became an important part of modern Danish society.
There are still many cooperative businesses, for example Coop and Arla, although most have by now moved far from their original basis, in both size and form of management.
The labour movement also set up businesses built on the cooperative idea.

The vast majority of the labour movement's businesses have today been outcompeted by private businesses.

The urban middle class had not only led the fight for a democratic constitution, but also the national line that had led Denmark into the war.
So the middle class stood weak.
This played into the hands of conservative circles backed by the country's landowners.
In 1866 they pushed through a change to the constitution, which was a democratic step backwards.
The king and the men with the highest incomes now got the right to elect most of the seats in one of the Rigsdag's chambers, the Landsting.
The somewhat broader right to vote was kept for the Folketing.
But the new constitution did not say how to act when the Folketing and the Landsting, which now had two quite different electorates, and thus two different political majorities, could not agree.
At the end of the 1800s the political fight between the right-wing and left-wing forces in the Rigsdag grew harder.

The period is therefore called the Constitutional Struggle, Forfatningskampen.
Around 1870 they organised themselves into two political parties, Højre and Venstre.

Estrup was head of government, the council president, from 1875 to 1894.

According to the parliamentary principle, it is solely the Folketing that decides who should have government power.
A government must not have a majority in the Folketing against it.

After long political struggles, Venstre took over government power for the first time in 1901.

It was especially academics and cottagers who voted for the new party.
In 1915 to 16, the old landowners' party Højre reorganised under the name the Conservative People's Party, Det Konservative Folkeparti.

On one side stood the Social Democrats, who put great emphasis on economic redistribution between rich and poor.
On the other side were the centre-right parties Venstre and the Conservative People's Party, which more wanted low taxes and economic freedom.
In the middle of this discussion stood the Social Liberal Party.
In its history, though, the party has cooperated most with the Social Democrats.

It was also at the end of the 1800s that the fight for equality really began.
The association Dansk Kvindesamfund, the Danish Women's Society, Denmark's oldest women's organisation, was founded in 1871.
It was decisive for the series of major advances in women's rights up to the 1920s.

In 1921, women gained equal access to most public positions, except in the military and as priests.

From 1908, women also got the vote for parish and town councils.

Worldwide, Denmark was among the first countries to introduce the vote for women in parliamentary elections.

In September 1939, Hitler's attack on Poland led Great Britain and France to declare war on Germany.
The Second World War had broken out in Europe.
Denmark was occupied by Germany from 1940 until the end of the war in 1945.
Denmark cooperated with the Germans to soften the terms of the occupation.
But during the war a Danish resistance movement grew up.
And at the same time, Denmark succeeded in saving the vast majority of the country's Jews from Nazi Germany's genocide, the Holocaust.
Let's start on the morning it happened.
Denmark and Norway were attacked and occupied by the German military on the ninth of April, 1940.
The German explanation was that Germany wanted to protect the two countries against a British occupation.
But Germany's occupation of Denmark was mainly because it was interested in Norway.
German warfare depended on deliveries of iron ore from Northern Sweden, which was to be shipped out through the town of Narvik on the ice-free Norwegian Atlantic coast.
The British had also shown interest in that supply of raw materials.
In addition, Germany wanted its access to the world's oceans secured via Norway's long coast.
Since Denmark is the country that lies between Norway and Germany, the Germans needed access to the airfield in Aalborg as a stopover.
Finally, Denmark's position on the North Sea made the country an indispensable part of the German defence against a possible Allied invasion of the European west coast.
Early in the morning of the ninth of April, the attack began, as German troops crossed the border in South Jutland.
Denmark's military resistance to the attack was insignificant and lasted only a few hours.
This meant that only a few Danish soldiers lost their lives in the attack.
Germany's military power was so great that the government did not think it would be of any use to continue resisting.
Germany demanded that Denmark should cooperate with the occupying power.
Denmark agreed to this out of necessity.
The Danish government was not deposed, but continued as a coalition government under Social Democratic leadership, though under German control.
The king also continued as regent.
Formally, Denmark kept its status as a sovereign, neutral state, even though the country was occupied by German troops.
And for most Danes, at least the first years of the occupation, life continued largely without big changes.
On the tenth of May, 1940, one month after the Danish surrender, France was also invaded by Germany, which defeated the French forces in less than six weeks.
This left Great Britain almost alone in the fight against Hitler, and an Allied victory seemed far away.
But German warfare met increasing problems as the years went by, and more and more people began to believe in an Allied victory.
Two events in 1941 were decisive in this connection.
One was Germany's invasion, Operation Barbarossa, of the Soviet Union on the twenty-second of June.
The other, when Japan, which was on Germany's side in the war, bombed the American fleet at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii in the Pacific on the seventh of December.
Thereby both the Soviet Union and the USA were drawn into the war on the Allied side, and Germany had gained too many and too strong enemies for it to be possible to win the war in the long run.
In the first years of the occupation, there was relative calm in Denmark in spite of the war.
But from 1942, the Danes' resistance to the German presence in the country began to grow.
The Germans thought neither that the Danish government did enough to crush this resistance, nor that it otherwise helped secure German interests in the country.

After a major crisis in the Danish-German relationship in October 1942, a new government was formed at German demand, led by Erik Scavenius, a former foreign minister and a strong advocate of the policy of cooperation with Germany.
In August 1943, when it was becoming more and more clear that Germany would lose the war, big strikes broke out in several Danish towns as a result of ever harsher German demands.

On the twenty-ninth of August, 1943, the government decided to submit its resignation to the king, after Scavenius had rejected the Germans' demand to intervene actively against the strikes and the ever-growing resistance to the German occupation, including the German demand for the death penalty for sabotage.
This ended the Danish government's policy of cooperation with Nazi Germany.
The German occupying power at the same time dissolved the Danish military.
The Danish navy itself sank most of its ships in 1943, so that they would not fall into German hands.
After that, Denmark in reality had no government, even though the king had refused to accept the government's resignation.
In practice, the country was afterwards run by the permanent secretaries, the departementschefer, the ministries' top administrative heads.

They continued, to a certain extent and more informally, the coordination with the German occupying power, to protect the population as much as possible despite the new and more serious situation in the country.
In 1940, about eight thousand Jews lived in Denmark.
More than seven thousand of them managed to flee the Nazis' persecution during the occupation.
Most were helped to Sweden by fellow Danish citizens, just before the Germans tried to arrest the Danish Jews in October 1943.
Up to five hundred Danish Jews were, however, sent to concentration camps in Germany, where many died.
On a European scale, a very large share of the Danish Jews survived this genocide, which is also known as the Holocaust.
In total, Nazi Germany murdered six million of Europe's roughly nine to ten million Jews during the war, most by mass shootings or in gas chambers in extermination camps.
And a different part of the kingdom took its own path in these years.
In 1944, Iceland broke away for good after 564 years under Denmark.

In the second half of the 1800s a strong independence movement arose in Iceland, which in 1918, with the so-called Act of Union, had gained extensive self-government in a federation, a personal union, with Denmark.
That means the Danish king was also king of Iceland.
Further, Iceland's foreign and defence policy was handled by Denmark.
During the Second World War, Iceland's geographical position in the middle of the northern Atlantic took on great importance.
Planes and ships on the way from the USA to Europe could use the island as a base.
Great Britain therefore occupied Iceland in May 1940, to prevent a German invasion.
Later in the war, the USA took over the defence of the Icelandic area.
The Act of Union from 1918 expired in 1943, and Denmark, being under German occupation, had no real possibility to renegotiate it.
In a referendum, an almost unanimous Icelandic population decided on full independence.
The Republic of Iceland was proclaimed on the seventeenth of June, 1944, which therefore became Iceland's national day.

Back in Denmark, the last years of the occupation were marked by more and more acts of sabotage, both against the German military in Denmark and against the Danes who cooperated with the occupying power.
The Freedom Council, Frihedsrådet, was established in September 1943.
It was an illegal committee in which the leaders of the various resistance movements coordinated the resistance against the German occupying power.
A big strike in Copenhagen in July 1944 gave rise to increased contact between the resistance movement and politicians.
After the strike, the Freedom Council and the Danish politicians cooperated to get Denmark recognised as an ally in the fight against Germany.
The Soviet Union opposed this, however.
In the spring of 1945, Nazi Germany collapsed after hard fighting in Europe.
On the fifth of May, Denmark was officially liberated by British forces, after the German troops had surrendered.
On Bornholm, however, the Germans refused to surrender.
In the last days of the occupation, the island was therefore attacked by Soviet forces, who stayed on the island until the spring of 1946.
In total, about seven thousand Danes were killed during the Second World War, many of them seamen who sailed in Allied war service.
Denmark was thus not as hard hit by the Second World War as many other European countries.
With about sixty million dead worldwide, the Second World War is the bloodiest war in world history, and the death toll was far higher in almost all other German-occupied countries.
For example, the Netherlands lost about two hundred thousand citizens, and in Eastern Europe, where the war was far bloodier than in Western Europe, Poland alone lost five to six million citizens.
The relatively low death toll and limited destruction are due, first, to the quick Danish surrender in April 1940 and the subsequent policy of cooperation with the Germans.
Second, it is because the German troops in Denmark, apart from those on Bornholm, surrendered without a fight at the end of the war in 1945, even before the Allied forces arrived in the country.
The war's main battles between the great powers thus never reached Denmark.
There was, however, a shortage of many goods in Denmark.

To control consumption, and to distribute the scarce supplies to everyone, so-called rationing was introduced for, for example, petrol, gas, electricity, sugar, coffee, tea, flour, bread, soap, meat and butter.
It meant that each citizen could only buy a limited amount of these goods.

Several of the winters during the occupation were unusually cold, with temperatures down to minus thirty degrees, and the lack of fuel, for example oil and coal, made it hard to heat homes, schools and workplaces.
But unlike in many other countries, there was never famine in Denmark.
The political system also survived the war.
The resistance movement gained a certain political influence in the time right after the liberation, but the old politicians and parties quickly returned to power.

After the Second World War, Denmark changed a lot.
Denmark gave up its traditional policy of neutrality and became a member of NATO in 1949.
Domestically too, the post-war period brought great changes, not least because of the rapidly growing economic prosperity.
Danes got more money in their hands than ever before.
Towards the end of the 1960s, disagreements between younger and older generations grew, because more young people questioned many of society's traditional norms.
The world had become a different place after the Second World War.
Millions of people had been killed during the war, and many cities in Europe lay in ruins.
The war had created a strong wish to secure international peace and security.
In 1945, a number of countries therefore founded the United Nations, the UN.
Denmark was a member of the UN from the start, which was meant, among other things, to help prevent a new world war.
After the Second World War, the Cold War arose between the two new superpowers, the USA and the Soviet Union.

It was an ideological struggle and an arms race over, among other things, nuclear weapons, between the Western democracies based on liberal market economy on one side, and the communist countries based on planned economy on the other.

Europe was divided into a west and an east along a line that especially reflected which areas had been liberated from Nazi Germany in the Second World War, by the USA and Great Britain in the west, and by the Soviet Union in the east.
The division between east and west became known as the Iron Curtain.
The Cold War came to shape the world until the communist dictatorships in Eastern Europe fell around 1990.
Denmark had tried to remain neutral in international conflicts since the England Wars at the beginning of the 1800s.
But since the policy of neutrality could not prevent the German occupation in the Second World War, Denmark chose a side in the Cold War.
It felt better protected as a member of the defence alliance NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
In 1949 Denmark therefore became a member of NATO.
The alliance consisted of the USA, Canada, Turkey, and a number of Western European countries.
Central in the NATO treaty is Article 5, the so-called "musketeer oath".
It says that an armed attack on one member country shall be regarded as an attack on all the member countries.
This obliges the other NATO countries, if necessary also with military force, to help the country that has been attacked.
Remember it: Article 5, the musketeer oath.
Opposite NATO stood the Warsaw Pact, which was founded in 1955.
This defence alliance was led by the communist Soviet Union, which got great influence over the countries of Eastern Europe after the Second World War.
After almost one hundred years under Germany's influence, Denmark's foreign and security policy after the Second World War was oriented especially towards the USA.
The USA played an important role in the rebuilding of Western Europe after the Second World War.
In the years 1948 to 51, the USA gave very large sums of money to several Western European countries, among others Denmark.
The money was given as part of the Marshall Plan, named after the American foreign minister George Marshall.
The purpose of the Marshall Aid was to get international trade, which had come to a halt during the Second World War, going again.
In that way, they also hoped to prevent communism from spreading further in Western Europe.
The economic help from the USA contributed to modernising Danish agriculture in the first decades after the Second World War.
Hundreds of thousands of horses were replaced by tractors, combine harvesters and other machines.
A large part of the workforce in the countryside therefore became superfluous, and many people moved from the rural areas into the towns in the 1950s.
The first election after the war, in 1945, resulted in a centre-right government under Venstre's leadership, but in 1947 the Social Democrats regained government power.

The Communist Party of Denmark, DKP, got relatively large support with twelve and a half percent of the votes at the election in 1945, because large parts of the population sympathised with the fact that many Danish communists had taken part in the resistance struggle during the occupation, and with the Soviet Union's considerable effort in defeating Nazi Germany.
Most of the party's new voters, however, quickly left it again.
The vast majority of voters continued to vote for the four old parties: the Social Democrats, the Social Liberal Party, the Conservative People's Party and Venstre.
The Danish tradition of political stability and agreement on the basic democratic rules of the game continued during the Cold War.
The Soviet-supported communists never gained a share of government power in Denmark.
In the post-war period, people began again to discuss whether there was a need to change the constitution.
In a referendum in 1953, a majority voted to change the constitution.
The change meant, among other things, that the Landsting was abolished.
Instead, a so-called one-chamber system was introduced, with the Folketing as the only legislative assembly.
In addition, the constitution now also applied to Greenland, and not only to Denmark and the Faroe Islands.
The succession to the throne was also changed, so that the Danish throne could pass to a woman.
However, sons still came before daughters, which means a younger son would still inherit the throne if he had an older sister.
The question of a female succession was particularly pressing because the then king, Frederik the Ninth, who reigned from nineteen forty-seven to seventy-two, had three daughters and no sons.

The constitutional change in 1953 thereby made it possible for his eldest daughter, the later Queen Margrethe the Second, who reigned from nineteen seventy-two to twenty twenty-four, to inherit the throne.
With a change to the Act of Succession in 2009, men and women got completely equal right of inheritance to the throne, so that it is always the eldest, son or daughter, who inherits the throne.
It was the Social Democrats who had the greatest political influence in the first decades after the Second World War.
From 1953 to 1968, all governments in Denmark were led by the Social Democrats.
The only party that emerged in this period, and which is still in the Folketing, is SF, the Socialist People's Party.

SF was formed in 1959 by a group of people who left DKP in protest against the communist countries' oppression of their populations, which the breakaways did not think DKP distanced itself enough from.
The crushing of the popular uprising against communist rule in Hungary in 1956 was decisive for the split of DKP.
From the end of the 1950s there was high economic growth in Europe, including in Denmark, which in the period 1957 to 73 had an economic boom almost without parallel in the country's history.
There was full employment and a big increase in production, just as most incomes grew steadily in this period.
The period has therefore often been called "the happy sixties", De glade 60'ere.
From the beginning of the 1960s, Denmark exported more industrial goods than agricultural goods.
It was also in this period that the building of the Danish welfare society really began, and an ever larger social safety net was spread under the population.
Several of the schemes that underlie today's Danish welfare society were established in those years, just as many of the existing schemes were considerably expanded.
The old-age pension, folkepensionen, which gives every citizen the right to a pension regardless of income, was for example introduced in 1956.

And in 1964, the Folketing decided that the municipalities must create the necessary number of day-care places, so that all families could have the opportunity to get their children into nursery and kindergarten.
The expansion of the welfare state also meant that taxes and duties rose a lot in this period.
The growth also meant that more labour was needed.
Many Danish women came out onto the labour market.
In the middle of the 1900s, the vast majority of married women had looked after house and children, while men went to work outside the home.
From the 1960s, women increasingly got education and work.
And many more children spent part of the day in one of the many new nurseries, kindergartens and after-school clubs that were set up.
Women, however, often got lower pay than men for the same work, and the fight to secure equality between men and women became stronger.
The economic growth meant that many more people suddenly got access to consumer goods beyond the most basic necessities such as food, clothes and housing.
TV sets, record players, fridges, freezers, washing machines, detached houses, cars and more had until then been regarded as luxury goods that only the richest could afford.
Now they became to a far greater extent part of most people's lives.

On top of the increased prosperity, the working week was continuously shortened, from forty-eight to forty hours between 1958 and 1974, and people got more holiday, from two to four weeks between 1953 and 1972.
So there were now far more people who had time and money to travel abroad on holiday or to buy a summer house.
And then the young people stood up.
At the end of the 1960s, in Denmark as in many other Western countries, there were clear tensions between the generations.
Young people's resistance to society's norms and authorities grew, and they therefore rebelled.
Many young people, especially in the bigger towns, broke with society's traditional norms and values.
Among other things, they questioned the USA's participation in the war in Vietnam, and the "nuclear family" with father, mother and children as society's supporting unit.
Instead came a freer attitude to sexual relations, also before marriage.
From 1966, the contraceptive pill could be sold legally in Denmark.
Women thereby gained access to an easy contraceptive, so that they themselves could control whether they wanted to become pregnant and have children.
The pill therefore became of decisive importance for women's sexual liberation.
New ways of living together also became more accepted.
For example, a couple could live together and have children without being married.
Some young people sought new ways of living together, among other things in communes.
The free town of Christiania in Copenhagen was established in 1971, when young people occupied an abandoned military barracks, Bådsmandsstræde Barracks.
After that, up to one thousand people settled in Christiania and tried to live out many of the new ideas of the time.
The free town of Christiania still exists.
The youth revolt also led to a student revolt.
In 1968 and the years after, many students and younger teachers rebelled against the so-called professor rule at the universities.
They demanded more influence, new forms of management and teaching, and a different content of the studies, and they succeeded in getting many of their demands through.
The stricter and more authoritarian upbringing of children in families and schools was also replaced by an education based on increased dialogue and cooperation between children and adults.
Among other things, it became completely forbidden in 1967 for teachers to hit pupils in the Danish folkeskole.
It was, however, thirty years later, in 1997, that it also became completely forbidden for parents to hit their own children.

After the golden years of the sixties, the story takes a turn.
Denmark became a member of the European Community, the EF, which was the forerunner of the present-day EU, in 1973.
And at the beginning of the 1970s, after many years of good economy and growth, Denmark, like many other countries, was hit by economic crisis.
The 1970s and 1980s became a period for Denmark of low economic growth, and of new political parties and movements.

In 1958, France, Italy, Germany and the Benelux countries, that is Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, began an economic cooperation, which developed into the European Community, the EF, and later into the European Union, the EU.
The purpose of the EF was to strengthen trade between the member countries, and to secure peace through strong cooperation.
Therefore, a common market was to be created between the EF countries, without customs borders or other obstacles to mutual trade.
The goal was also that all inhabitants should be free to seek and take work in other EF countries.
On the first of January, 1973, Denmark entered the EF.
A majority of sixty-three point three percent of the voters had said yes to membership in a referendum in October 1972.
In the run-up to the referendum, there was much debate on the EF question.
The supporters thought Denmark would become richer by taking part in the European economic cooperation.
They expected, first, that Denmark's then most important trading partner, Great Britain, would also join the EF together with Denmark.

Further, they wanted to secure the best possible opportunities to trade on the European market, and not least the German one, whose importance for the Danish economy had grown strongly in the preceding years.
In addition, it was an advantage to secure Danish agriculture access to the EF's agricultural support.
The opponents were against Denmark giving up some of its right to decide for itself.
They were afraid that the big countries would come to decide too much, and that membership would harm public welfare and Danish national identity.
Prime Minister Jens Otto Krag signed the Treaty of Rome in Brussels on the twenty-second of January, 1972.
Consideration for exports and the economy became decisive for the Danish yes.
Great Britain and Ireland became members of the EF at the same time as Denmark.
In 1986 there was a new referendum on strengthening cooperation in the EF.
The vote was about the European Single Act, or the "EF package", as it came to be called in Denmark.
Its purpose was to carry out an internal market, where goods, persons, services and capital could move freely across the borders between the member countries.
A majority of Danes, fifty-six point two percent, voted yes.
In 1974, Denmark, like many other Western countries, was hit by an economic crisis.
It was triggered by oil prices rising violently in 1973.
The background was that the Arab countries markedly increased the price of oil to put pressure on the Western countries that supported Israel in a war against Egypt and Syria, the Yom Kippur War.
Oil was absolutely crucial for the economy, as it was needed in most of industry, for cars and for heating homes.
Denmark at that time produced very little oil itself, which therefore had to be bought abroad.
So the price increase gave serious problems in Denmark, which already had a deficit in trade with other countries.
The previous years' high economic growth fell considerably, prices in the shops rose very quickly, many became unemployed, and the surplus on the state budget was turned into a deficit.

The problems were made worse and prolonged when another violent price increase on oil happened in 1979 to 80, due to unrest in Iran in connection with the Islamic revolution and the subsequent war between Iran and Iraq.

During the 1980s, the price of oil fell again, because more oil was extracted outside the Middle East, for example in the North Sea, and because part of the world's consumption of oil was replaced by other forms of energy, for example natural gas, coal, nuclear power and, to a much smaller extent, renewable energy sources such as wind power or solar energy.

Further, the oil crises contributed to creating an interest in energy-saving measures, such as better insulation of homes, and the development of cars and electronics, among others TV sets, fridges and freezers, that use energy more efficiently.
The 1970s were also a period of big political changes in Denmark.
Many voters protested against high taxes and against the bureaucracy that had followed with the large public sector in the welfare society, and voters got greater distrust of the politicians.
At the general election in 1973, voters suddenly voted markedly differently from before.
It was a big landslide, and this election is therefore called the Landslide Election, Jordskredsvalget.
The Social Democrats, the Social Liberal Party, Venstre, the Conservative People's Party and SF, the five parties then in the Folketing, all got far fewer votes.
Before the Landslide Election, ninety-three percent of voters had voted for one of the five parties.
After the election, it was only sixty-four percent.

Instead, voters voted five more parties into the Folketing, of which the largest was the protest party, the Progress Party, Fremskridtspartiet, which got sixteen percent of the votes, with the lawyer Mogens Glistrup at the head.
The party's main causes were to abolish income tax and public bureaucracy.
Many of the old parties' voters gradually returned over the next years, and none of the new parties that were elected in 1973 are still in the Folketing.

But the Landslide Election is a milestone in Danish political history, among other things because afterwards, between seven and twelve parties have been elected to the Folketing at each election, rather than typically five or six before 1973.

Even though new parties have continually emerged, it has always been politicians from either the Social Democrats, the Social Liberal Party, the Conservative People's Party or Venstre who have been prime ministers in Denmark since the Change of System in 1901.
In the 1970s, successive Danish governments tried to turn around the economic downturn, but without much success.
At the beginning of the 1980s, Denmark had a large deficit on the trade balance, that is, the relation between the value of what Denmark buys and sells abroad.
At the same time, around ten percent of the labour force was out of work.
An important cause of the economic crisis was a large debt to other countries.
The Social Democrats had, with only shorter interruptions, sat in government and held the prime minister's post most of the time since 1929.
But in 1982, because of difficulties solving the economic problems, they left government power to the centre-right wing, without there having been a general election.
The prime minister became the conservative Poul Schlüter, who was prime minister for more than ten years, until 1993.
Poul Schlüter is the first and so far only prime minister from the Conservative People's Party.

This is because Venstre has most of the time been the largest centre-right party since the Change of System in 1901, and therefore has normally held the prime minister's post when there have been centre-right governments after 1901.
The change of government in 1982 is, furthermore, a historic milestone, because the centre-right parties have since most often been in power.

In the period 1982 to 2022, the centre-right parties Venstre and the Conservative People's Party together sat in government and held the prime minister's post for a total of twenty-four years, and the Social Democrats for a total of sixteen years.
The Schlüter government gradually managed to improve the Danish economy, especially in the second half of the 1980s.
The price was record-high unemployment at the start of the 1990s.
But inflation, the price increases, which had been a big problem in the 1970s, fell, and from 1990 there was a surplus on the trade balance against other countries.
This meant that healthy economic growth could get going.
In this context, it also helped that Denmark became more self-sufficient in oil from the North Sea.
The Schlüter government also abolished DR's monopoly, that is its exclusive right, to broadcast Danish TV, which DR had had since the first Danish television broadcast in 1948.
In 1986 it was thus made legal for private parties to own TV channels, and the same year the Folketing decided to establish TV 2, which broadcast for the first time in 1988.
In the following years, the number of radio and TV channels in Denmark grew considerably, and cable and satellite TV with many foreign channels became a significant part of the Danish media picture.
And finally, movements from the grass roots.
After women had begun to come out onto the labour market from the middle of the 1960s, many women in the 1970s demanded more equality as a continuation of this.
For example, women in the Red Stocking movement, rødstrømpebevægelsen, fought through political actions for better conditions for women.
Throughout the 1970s, equality was a very hot political topic.
In 1976, the Folketing, on the basis of an EF directive, passed a law on equal pay for the same work.
Free access to abortion was another of the women's movement's political goals.
Previously it had only been possible to get an abortion if there was a special reason, for example consideration for the woman's health.
But in 1973 the Folketing decided that Danish women should themselves be able to choose whether to terminate a pregnancy.
Until the twelfth week of pregnancy, women could freely choose to have an abortion.
Opposition to free abortion was a significant reason why the Christian People's Party, which is now called the Christian Democrats, was formed and elected to the Folketing in 1973.
But free abortion still applies, and in 2025 the limit for free abortion was raised from the twelfth to the eighteenth week of pregnancy.
Several grassroots movements were very active in the 1970s.
Grassroots movements were usually groups that worked to achieve one particular political goal.
The peace movement was active in this period, and worked, among other things, against military armament and the arms race between the great powers.
Thousands of Danes also demonstrated against nuclear power.
The popular resistance was an important reason why the Folketing in 1985 decided to plan the future energy supply in Denmark without nuclear power.

Not least a serious accident at the nuclear power plant Chernobyl in the Soviet Union, in present-day Ukraine, the year after, in 1986, has been of great importance for the later reluctance towards nuclear power.
The anti-nuclear power movement's international emblem originates from the Danish branch of the movement.

The latest years' climate crisis and high energy prices have, however, created a renewed political discussion on whether Denmark should nevertheless introduce nuclear power in some form, just as a larger part of the population has become more positive towards nuclear power.

Danish history since 1990 has stood under the sign of globalisation.
The Berlin Wall and the Iron Curtain fell, and new conflicts broke out.
The fight against terrorism has also marked the world and Denmark, and Denmark has played a new and more active role in international affairs.
The EF expanded its political cooperation and was renamed the European Union, the EU, but Danes embraced the new EU only hesitantly.
The country's economic situation, though interrupted by a financial crisis in 2008, improved again, and problems integrating refugees and immigrants into society occupied more and more people.
And in 2020, a global health crisis hit with Covid-19.
Let's start with the fall of a system.
Around 1990, the communist system in Eastern Europe collapsed.
The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, in November, and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, meant the end of the Cold War.
It brought big changes in Europe.
Central and Eastern European countries that had earlier lain behind the Iron Curtain now moved politically closer to Western Europe.
Denmark got close ties especially to the three Baltic countries: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
After the Cold War, new conflicts broke out, among others in Iraq and in the former Yugoslavia.
From now on Denmark took part more actively in international conflicts and became involved in several of these wars.
After Iraq had occupied Kuwait in 1990, Denmark sent a warship to help enforce the international community's trade blockade against Iraq.
In its place arose a number of independent states, which quickly came into conflict with each other.
Danish soldiers were stationed as UN forces, in Bosnia and Croatia, in the middle of the 1990s.
They were to help create peace between the parties to the conflict.
Kosovo, which at that time was a province in Yugoslavia, was also hit by conflict in 1999.
Here Danish fighter planes took part in NATO's actions.
Denmark's relationship with European cooperation was marked by political disagreement in the 1990s.
In 1992, the twelve member countries agreed to expand the cooperation, and the EF changed its name to the EU, the European Union.

The name change reflected that the cooperation, which until then had been cooperation on economic questions such as trade, agriculture and fisheries, was expanded with a broader range of political areas of cooperation.
A majority in the Folketing was in favour of Denmark taking part in the expanded cooperation.
But according to the constitution, it was necessary to hold a referendum.

In June 1992, a small majority of the population, fifty point seven percent, voted no to the Maastricht Treaty, as the union agreement came to be called, because it was concluded in the town of Maastricht in the Netherlands.
In 1993, a majority of the population, fifty-six point seven percent, voted yes to the so-called Edinburgh Agreement, which meant that Denmark got four so-called opt-outs, forbehold, from the EU.

That means that Denmark did not take part in the EU's cooperation in the following four areas: Union citizenship, the common currency (the euro), the defence area, and the cooperation on a common justice and immigration policy.
Only two of the four opt-outs still apply today: the euro, and justice and immigration.
Therefore Denmark, for example, still has its own national currency, the krone, whereas most EU countries have the common currency, the euro.
And Denmark also does not take part in the EU's common justice and immigration policy.

The opposition to the EU in parts of the population also became one of the reasons why the Red-Green Alliance, Enhedslisten, which in 1989 had been formed as a coming together of a number of smaller left-wing parties, was elected to the Folketing for the first time in 1994.
Despite the EU opt-outs, a clear majority of the Danish population is positive towards Danish membership of the EU.
In 1993, the Social Democrats came to power again, with Poul Nyrup Rasmussen as the new prime minister.
The economic problems Denmark experienced in the 1970s and 1980s turned into an economic upturn.
In the middle of the 1990s, economic growth rose again, and more people got jobs.
In addition, the production of oil and gas from the Danish fields in the North Sea meant that Denmark gradually got a net export of oil.
That contributed to the surplus on the trade balance getting bigger, and the debt to other countries gradually being paid off.
The debate on immigration to Denmark took up more and more space during the 1990s.

The number of persons with an immigrant background had risen a lot in the preceding decades, and in the bigger Danish towns, districts had emerged where many residents had an ethnic background other than Danish.
At the same time, many refugees and immigrants found it difficult to get education and work.

The question of integration got great political attention in this period, among other things because relatively many people with a foreign background in Denmark did poorly in the education system, and because a relatively large share was without work and received social benefits such as cash benefit, kontanthjælp, and early retirement pension, førtidspension.
Many Danes also thought that some immigrants had a culture that was very different from the Danes', and that they were not always good enough at learning the Danish language.

The wish for tightening of the foreigners and integration policy among many Danes was of great importance for the Danish People's Party, Dansk Folkeparti, with party founder and party leader Pia Kjærsgaard, born 1947, at the head, being elected to the Folketing for the first time in 1998.
Pia Kjærsgaard led the party from 1995 to 2012, and from 2015 to 2019 she was the first woman to be Speaker of the Folketing.
The Danish People's Party contributed to the foreigners policy becoming an important theme at the general elections in the following decades.
Other political parties, however, also gradually took up the subject.
Poul Nyrup Rasmussen was prime minister from 1993 to 2001.
In 2001, the centre-right parties regained government power.
The prime minister became Anders Fogh Rasmussen from Venstre, prime minister from 2001 to 2009.
Discussions about foreigners and integration continued, and the new government carried through several tightenings of the foreigners policy.
The aim was to limit parts of immigration, get more people into work and improve integration.
Some of the following governments have carried through further tightenings of the foreigners policy.
For example, a requirement has been introduced that you must have stayed for a longer period in Denmark and have worked before you can receive full cash benefit.
In addition, foreigners must have lived longer in Denmark to get Danish citizenship, the indfødsret, just as they must meet requirements for work and self-support.
Further, you must not commit serious crime, and you must pass a series of tests in the Danish language and in Danish history, society, culture and values.
That, of course, is the very test you are preparing for.
It has also become harder to bring a spouse from abroad to Denmark.

Among other things, both persons must be at least twenty-four years old, the so-called twenty-four-year rule, and meet a series of requirements regarding, among other things, work, self-support, education, housing and Danish language skills.
The aim is to secure the best possible starting point for successful integration of the spouse who comes to Denmark.
But not everyone has agreed on the stricter foreigners policy.

Opponents have criticised, among other things, that the lower financial benefits create increased poverty, and that the stricter requirements for family reunification split families, and have made it too difficult, also for Danish citizens, to get a spouse into the country.
The international community changed rapidly at the beginning of the new millennium.
The global economy and international terrorism confronted Denmark with new challenges.
After the terror attack on the USA on the eleventh of September, 2001, combating terrorism became an important task in most countries.
This has especially led to increased cooperation between intelligence services, but also to military interventions, in which Denmark has taken an active part.
Behind the attack on the USA in 2001 were terrorists who operated from Afghanistan, in understanding with the then Afghan regime.
In 2002 the Folketing decided to send Danish soldiers to Afghanistan to take part in an American-led effort.
In 2003 the USA attacked Iraq to remove the Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein and Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction.
Again, the Danish government backed it and sent Danish soldiers.
One of Denmark's biggest foreign policy crises in recent times developed after the newspaper Jyllands-Posten in 2005 printed twelve caricature drawings of the Muslim prophet Muhammad.
The newspaper printed the drawings because it had heard that some illustrators did not dare to draw Muhammad for fear of being attacked or killed.
The caricature drawings led to big protests both in Denmark and abroad.
In many Muslim countries there were big demonstrations, where, among other things, the Dannebrog was set on fire, and in a few places, in Syria and Lebanon, also Danish embassies and consulates.
A number of countries also boycotted Danish products because of the drawings.
Jyllands-Posten was in 2008 acquitted in a defamation case brought by a number of Muslim organisations.
The debate about freedom of expression did not end there, however.
In 2010, an attempt was made to murder one of the illustrators in his home.

In 2015, Denmark was hit by a terror attack in Copenhagen, where a man who sympathised with the terror organisation Islamic State shot and killed a film-maker while he took part in a debate meeting about "Art, blasphemy and freedom of expression" at Østerbro.
Later the same day, the terrorist tried to force his way into the Jewish synagogue in central Copenhagen.
In the attack, a Jewish guard was shot and killed outside the synagogue.
The terrorist was afterwards himself killed in an exchange of fire with the police.

After about fifteen years of economic growth and progress, Denmark was in 2008 hit by the international financial crisis.

When the crisis set in, unemployment was the lowest in thirty years, and there was a large surplus on the state budget.
It was turned into a deficit, but Denmark was still not hit by as big problems with state deficits and debt as most other EU countries.

At the same time, Denmark's foreign debt has turned into a large claim, so that other countries owe Denmark more money than the other way around, and the surplus on the trade balance has set repeated records in the last twenty years.
In 2025, the surplus was about three hundred eighty-two billion kroner.

In 2024, the Danish state's revenue was thus one hundred thirty-three billion kroner higher than expenditure.

Now, the challenge for the welfare state.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen was in 2009 elected the new Secretary General of the defence alliance NATO.
He was succeeded as prime minister by his party colleague Lars Løkke Rasmussen of Venstre, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2011, and again from 2015 to 2019.

Two years later, in 2011, the Social Democrats regained power, and Helle Thorning-Schmidt became Denmark's first female prime minister, for the next four years until 2015, when Lars Løkke Rasmussen again became prime minister.
The challenge of moving more people from transfer income and into the labour market has been the motive for numerous Danish welfare reforms over the last thirty to thirty-five years.
Both Lars Løkke Rasmussen's and Helle Thorning-Schmidt's governments headed many such reforms.
One of the biggest long-term challenges for the welfare state in European countries is that there will be fewer people to pay for the welfare that more people are to enjoy.
This is first and foremost because people on average live longer.
As in other Western countries, life expectancy rises by a couple of months every year.
That development is expected to continue.
At the same time, the birth rate has fallen, while expectations of the quality of elderly care and the health service are rising.
That means there will be markedly more elderly people in relation to the number of fifteen to sixty-four-year-olds, and fewer to work and pay for welfare.
At the same time, working life starts later because of more education.
All in all, there is a lack of labour in many places on the Danish labour market, even though there are still people out of work.
Many different reforms have therefore aimed at increasing the labour supply, to get more people to work, earn money and pay tax.

In this connection, the period in which one can receive support as unemployed from an unemployment insurance fund, the A-kasse, has gradually been shortened since the 1990s and since the last reform in the area in 2010 has been two years.
The so-called Retirement Reform from 2011 was meant to ensure a faster and bigger rise in how old people typically were when they withdraw from the labour market.
Further, reforms were agreed in 2012 and 2013 respectively that should ensure that fewer people go on early retirement pension, and that fewer are on cash benefit.
A number of tax reforms have also had the declared goal of increasing the labour supply by lowering tax on labour income.
Students have, through a series of reforms, been encouraged to start their studies earlier and finish them faster.
A significant challenge in the years 2020 to 22 was a global pandemic with Covid-19, which was caused by the so-called coronavirus.
The virus was discovered in China in 2019.
In Denmark the first case was registered in February 2020.
The government, the Folketing, the Danish Health Authority and others tried to contain the disease through a series of recommendations and restrictions.
They were to ensure that people, for example, did not meet too many other people, that they kept distance from each other and that they washed their hands in sanitiser.
A main purpose of the restrictions was to prevent too many people being infected at once, so that the hospitals were not overloaded by many admissions.
Therefore, you had to wear face masks on buses, trains and in shops, among other things.
You also could not travel as freely between Denmark and abroad as normal.
Schools were also closed in periods, and pupils were taught at home via the internet.
In addition, many restaurants, cafés, museums and theatres were closed in periods, and football matches and other sports took place without spectators, just as many worked from home.
The health service tested thousands of people daily to find the infected, who then had to stay home for some time so they did not infect more.
The coronavirus has mutated several times into ever more contagious variants, and the disease has so far hit the country in three big waves.
An important means of fighting the disease in the long term was to vaccinate the population.
It took only about one year from the outbreak of the disease to develop vaccines against coronavirus, and in December 2020 the first Dane was vaccinated.
Since then, most, about ninety percent of Denmark's population, have been vaccinated with two or three jabs.
Globally, almost seven million people were registered dead with coronavirus, including almost ten thousand in Denmark.
And finally, the political map today.
In recent years, more new parties have come into Danish politics.
Five of these, Liberal Alliance, the Alternative, the Denmark Democrats, the Moderates and the Citizens' Party, were elected to the current Folketing.
Liberal Alliance was elected to the Folketing for the first time in 2011.
The party arose with a policy of more tax cuts, bigger economic incentive to work, lower public spending and more private market economy.
The Alternative, Alternativet, has, among other things, emphasised that greater focus should be put on the green area.

The Alternative was elected to the Folketing for the first time in 2015.
In addition, two parties, the Denmark Democrats and the Moderates, emerged shortly before the general election in 2022.

The Denmark Democrats was founded by former Minister for Immigration and Integration Inger Støjberg.
The party is critical of immigration to Denmark.

The Moderates were founded by former prime minister and party leader Lars Løkke Rasmussen.
